analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably excessive gasoline price hikes during oil-market emergencies the President declares.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Duckworth with 3 Democratic cosponsors, sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When the President proclaims an international crisis affecting oil markets, the bill would make it illegal to sell gasoline or other petroleum fuels at prices that are unconscionably excessive or that take unfair advantage of the crisis [S2][S3]. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with enhanced civil penalties up to $100 million or triple the profits gained, the Justice Department could pursue criminal fines up to $500 million with priority given to companies selling more than $10 billion in fuel a year, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents [S3]. Proclamations could cover the whole country and be renewed in 30-day blocks [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and other fuel buyers, including farms, businesses, and homeowners, would gain protection from price spikes that exceed what supply costs and market conditions justify during an oil-market emergency [S3]. State attorneys general would gain a new federal tool to sue on behalf of residents [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell gasoline at wholesale or retail at an unconscionably excessive price during a proclaimed international oil-market crisis, judged against the seller's own prior 30-day prices, competing local prices, and actual added costs or risks [S3].

Directs the FTC to prioritize enforcement against companies with over $10 billion a year in U.S. fuel sales, and authorizes civil penalties up to $100 million or three times the profits gained from a violation [S3].
Lets state attorneys general sue in federal court on behalf of residents for retail-level violations, and adds a criminal fine of up to $500 million enforceable by the Attorney General [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, wholesale fuel distributors, and large fuel retailers would bear the cost: exposure to civil penalties of up to $100 million or triple profits, criminal fines up to $500 million, and litigation from state attorneys general during declared emergencies [S3]. Small sellers with genuinely higher supply costs are protected by the bill's factors, which exclude price increases that reflect added costs or risks outside the seller's control [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners and large fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: Price caps during shortages can blunt the price signal that encourages conservation and new supply; the bill tries to address this by treating increased supply to the affected area as a factor and excluding sellers whose prices reflect real added costs, but critics of gouging laws argue any cap risks shortages or lines at the pump during a crisis [S3].

The standard — 'unconscionably excessive' pricing that takes 'unfair advantage' — is a vague legal test, and the President could declare a crisis covering the entire country and renew it indefinitely in 30-day periods, a broad grant of discretion that would apply federal penalties to ordinary market pricing decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside during a declared emergency is real protection against outlier price increases not explained by costs, with enforcement aimed first at the largest companies and an explicit safe harbor for sellers whose costs genuinely rose [S3]. The costs are the risks inherent in any emergency price cap — weaker supply incentives and a vaguely defined standard — plus a significant expansion of presidential and federal enforcement power; whether that trade is worth it depends heavily on how narrowly future presidents use the proclamation authority [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on March 24, 2022, during the gas price spike that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its last action of record [S5].
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners, wholesale fuel distributors, and large retail fuel sellers, who face no new federal anti-gouging penalties or state attorney general suits during oil-market emergencies, and drivers remain protected only by the patchwork of state gouging laws that existed before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil refiners and large fuel sellers

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: 50 of 100 Senate seats; no Republican cosponsored
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsorship; the bill drew no Republican support in its only public stage.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with 3 of 48 Democrats cosponsoring, the bill never built the support needed to move in a 50-50 Senate.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and major fuel wholesalers
industries.note: The bill would expose them to civil penalties up to $100 million or triple profits, criminal fines up to $500 million, and priority FTC and DOJ enforcement during declared oil-market emergencies, with the largest companies (over $10 billion in U.S. fuel sales) targeted first [S3]. Because the bill died, no new federal penalty exposure was created.

industries.industry: Retail gasoline stations and fuel retailers
industries.note: Retail sales to motorists and direct end users fall squarely under the ban, and state attorneys general could sue retailers directly on behalf of residents; small sellers are shielded by the bill's cost-and-risk safe harbor, but large chains would face litigation risk during emergencies [S3].
